items.item: Catalog of 19 classical-to-LLM NLP tasks (classification, NER, MT, summarization, QA, generation, topic modeling, similarity, dialog, normalization, relation extraction, code generation, style transfer, entailment, knowledge-augmented generation, simplification, multimodal generation, emotion recognition, role playing)
items.notes: Section 1.1 lists six core NLP tasks in Table 1.1.1; the slide expands the catalog to 19. Tasks missing from the book or only mentioned in passing: topic modeling, text normalization, relation extraction, style transfer, text simplification, multimodal text generation, emotion recognition (vs binary sentiment), and text-based role playing. A short catalogue callout summarizing the full 19-task taxonomy would close the gap.

items.item: Healthcare LLM applications, split into professional-facing (clinical documentation, radiology, triage, etc.) vs patient-facing (lab results, symptom assessment, medication adherence, etc.)
items.notes: Book has no domain-application overview. A short Healthcare/Cybersecurity/Software Engineering tri-domain figure (or callout) would broaden the motivation in Section 1.1.

items.item: Cybersecurity LLM applications: nine application families plus 5-branch 'opportunities due to LLMs' tree (vulnerability detection, content classification, explainability, data challenges, LLM-risk mitigation including guardrails/deepfakes/adversarial examples)
items.notes: Book does not catalogue cybersecurity LLM uses anywhere in Ch 1. Worth a single 'domain panorama' callout that also acknowledges LLMs are part of the attack surface, not only the defense.

items.item: Five-petal SE-lifecycle map of LLM use: documentation, code generation, testing/debugging, code review/optimization, synthetic data generation
items.notes: Book mentions code generation as one task but does not show the full SE-lifecycle decomposition; useful for the 'audience is developers' framing.

items.item: Whitespace + regex baseline tokenizers; Spacy / NLTK off-the-shelf tokenizers; explicit 'build a vocabulary' step
items.notes: Section 1.2 jumps straight from preprocessing to BoW; it does not show the naive whitespace/regex pipeline that motivates the open-vocabulary problem. A short 3-step ramp (whitespace -> regex -> off-the-shelf) before BoW would mirror the slide's pedagogical motivation for subwords.

items.item: Special tokens roster: <|pad|>, <|sep|>, <|endoftext|>, with the convention that each model defines its own
items.notes: Section 1.7 covers special tokens in detail (Table 1.7.1). Slide adds nothing the book does not have.

items.item: Classical vocabulary-reduction recipe (case folding, stemming, lemmatization, stop-word removal) is essential for statistics-based features but usually NOT used with modern LLMs
items.notes: Section 1.2 covers all four operations and explicitly notes modern LLMs skip them. Already at greater depth than slide.

items.item: Three-way comparison: word-level (vocab explosion, treats work/working/worked as unrelated) vs character-level (tiny vocab, no semantics) vs sub-word (compromise)
items.notes: Section 1.5 has this comparison with Figure 1.5.2 and a numeric experiment.

items.item: BPE algorithm: start with chars; (a) find most frequent adjacent pair, (b) create new token, (c) replace; merges applied in learned order; distinction of mid-word vs end-of-word tokens (e.g., `er` vs `er\w`)
items.notes: Section 1.6 covers the algorithm in depth with Figure 1.6.1 and a from-scratch lab in Section 1.8.

items.item: WordPiece marks within-word continuation tokens with `##` prefix (e.g., unhappy -> un + ##happy)
items.notes: Section 1.8 head-to-head tokenizer comparison shows BERT outputs with `##` prefixes; concept is also discussed in Section 1.6.

items.item: BoW and TF-IDF as sparse vocabulary-length vectors with the running example of movie reviews
items.notes: Section 1.2 covers both with worked examples.

items.item: Naive Bayes text classification on BoW features (each word votes independently for a class)
items.notes: Section 1.1 mentions Naive Bayes as a statistical-era technique but Section 1.2 does not actually walk through the per-word voting computation. Adding a brief NB demonstration on the BoW matrix would close the loop on the classical pipeline.

items.item: Vector-Space Model: documents as directions in N-dim space; classical search via inverted index ranked by TF-IDF similarity
items.notes: Section 1.2 has a 'Note: The Vector Space Model' callout that hits these points and connects to BM25.

items.item: Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA classifier): find a direction in N-dim space along which classes are maximally separated
items.notes: Book does not introduce LDA as a classical baseline classifier anywhere in Ch 1. Optional but cheap to add as a one-paragraph mention with the deck's class-separation visualization.

items.item: Confusion matrix, precision, recall as evaluation tools for text classification
items.notes: Book defers all evaluation metrics to a later chapter. A two-sentence pointer + matrix sketch inside Section 1.2 would close the loop on the classical-NLP narrative without duplicating Part 9.

items.item: Topic-vector representation as denser, semantically-meaningful alternative to BoW (e.g., 80% sport, 20% news); motivation that frequently co-occurring words belong to the same topic
items.notes: Book skips topic models entirely. This is the single biggest classical-NLP gap in Ch 1. A short subsection (1.2.x or 1.3.0) introducing topic vectors would bridge BoW/TF-IDF to dense embeddings more smoothly.

items.item: Document-Term Matrix (DTM) and Latent Semantic Analysis (LSA) via truncated SVD; rank = number of topics; document-topic matrix as input features for LDA classifier
items.notes: LSA / truncated-SVD topic models are nowhere in the book. Worth a short callout especially since LSA is still actively used in production search and a useful conceptual stepping stone to dense embeddings.

items.item: Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDiA): each topic is a distribution over words; each document is a mixture of topic distributions; number of topics is a hyperparameter swept via coherence/perplexity
items.notes: LDiA is not in Ch 1 (or anywhere in Part 1). Section 1.2 should briefly mention LDiA, even just as a forward reference, given it remains widely used and is conceptually paired with the Gibbs-sampling Ch 4.4 / 0006 deck.

items.item: Distributional hypothesis: a word is characterized by the company it keeps; semantically similar inputs should have similar dense representations
items.notes: Section 1.3 quotes Firth and walks through the distributional hypothesis in depth.

items.item: Word2Vec CBOW vs Skip-Gram architectures with side-by-side diagram; CBOW predicts center from context, Skip-Gram inverts the prediction with 5-15 token window
items.notes: Section 1.3 covers both, with focus on Skip-Gram. CBOW is mentioned in a callout.

items.item: cosmul similarity (Levy-Goldberg analogy scoring): ratio of products of positive to negative cosine distances
items.notes: Book covers cosine similarity exhaustively but never mentions cosmul. This is a low-cost addition (one formula + one Gensim usage example) that improves analogy demos.

items.item: Document classification via mean-pooled word embeddings; works for very short documents like tweets but better methods using sentence embeddings exist
items.notes: Book mentions sentence-transformers as a library shortcut but does not explicitly call out mean-pooled-Word2Vec as the first sentence-embedding baseline. Worth a one-line bridge between word embeddings and sentence embeddings.

items.item: Negative sampling for Skip-Gram: train on (context, target) pairs where wrong-word negatives receive low predicted probability, avoiding full-vocabulary softmax
items.notes: Section 1.3 covers negative sampling with the loss formula and an order-of-magnitude analysis (16000x speedup).

items.item: GloVe co-occurrence matrix factorization, loss J = sum f(X_ij) (w_i . w_j + b_i + b_j - log X_ij)^2
items.notes: Section 1.3 covers GloVe loss in equation form with the weighting function described.

items.item: Generalized embeddings: token sequences beyond language (graphs as node walks, songs as playlist sequences); end-to-end song-recommendation pipeline (build corpus from playlists, train Word2Vec, query nearest songs)
items.notes: Book misses the generalization angle entirely (graph walks, song recommendation, no-metadata embeddings). This is a memorable application example that would substantially strengthen Section 1.3's 'why embeddings matter beyond NLP' framing. Add as a 'Real-World Scenario' callout or short subsection.

items.item: Motivation: Word2Vec assigns a single average embedding per word, losing contextual nuance ('mouse' computer vs animal, pronouns 'he'/'she')
items.notes: Section 1.4 covers the polysemy problem with 'bank' as the canonical example and the same 'one vector per type vs token' framing.

items.item: Attention as soft lookup over values, with Q/K/V derived via W_Q, W_K, W_V projection matrices; concrete intuition ('Mouse' asks if it is alive; 'Clicked' offers action-on-static-object info)
items.notes: Section 2.3 covers Q/K/V abstraction with the soft-database-query mental model.

items.item: Scaled dot-product attention in matrix form softmax(QK^T / sqrt(d_k)) V with dimension annotations
items.notes: Section 2.3 has the full formula, scaling justification, and matrix-dimension trace.

items.item: Masked Language Modeling (MLM): attention + classifier head over masked-token context vector reconstructs the original token
items.notes: Section 1.4 introduces BERT but does not include the MLM diagram-with-classifier-head. Module 3.5 mentions BERT pretraining briefly. The book lacks a focused MLM-with-attention-and-classifier-head walkthrough that the slide provides; consider in Ch 1.4 or Part 2.

items.item: Attention dropout: randomly zero entries of the attention matrix to prevent over-reliance on frequent word combinations
items.notes: Book mentions dropout in the multi-head implementation but does not call out attention-matrix dropout as a specific regularization technique with motivation. Worth a one-sentence callout.

items.item: Multi-head attention with weight-splitting: single big matrix split along embedding dim (view+transpose) instead of separate per-head matrices; PyTorch class implementation
items.notes: Section 2.4 implements MHA from scratch with the combined qkv_proj fused projection and head splitting.

items.item: Cross-attention for seq2seq fusion: queries from target (English), keys/values from source (Spanish); stacks with self-attention
items.notes: Section 2.3 has the cross-vs-self comparison table.

items.item: Causal attention class with triangular mask + renormalization; the 'next token not yet available when contextualizing last token' motivation
items.notes: Section 2.3 covers causal masking with triangular structure and numeric demonstration.

items.item: Sparse attention patterns: full quadratic, sliding window, dilated sliding window, global tokens, random-token attention as a complement
items.notes: Section 3.5 covers sparse attention but only in passing. The slide's four-pattern catalogue (with the dilated-sliding-window and random-attention add-on from Longformer/BigBird) is more concrete. Worth a small comparison figure naming the patterns.

items.item: FFN structure: expand (linear up-projection) -> nonlinear -> contract (linear down-projection); inner dim ~4x embed dim; applied independently per token; FFN blends information across heads
items.notes: Section 3.1 covers FFN as the per-token nonlinear transformation.

items.item: ReLU vs GeLU motivation: ReLU 'pass if positive above threshold'; GeLU 'smooth gating, scale by positiveness, keep info on small negative values'
items.notes: Book mentions SwiGLU and GeGLU in Section 3.8 but does not give the prose intuition for why GeLU's smooth gating is preferred to ReLU. Add one-paragraph intuition to Section 3.1.

items.item: Residual connections stabilize training by preventing vanishing gradients; layer normalization (per-token zero-mean unit-variance + learnable gamma/beta) stabilizes by preventing exploding gradients; paired they enable gradient-stable training
items.notes: Section 3.1 covers residuals and LayerNorm with explicit gradient-stability motivation.

items.item: Pre-Norm vs Post-Norm: pre-norm places LayerNorm on the residual path before each sub-layer; gradients flow through an identity path; dominant in modern LLMs
items.notes: Section 3.5.5 covers Pre-LN vs Post-LN with the same identity-path intuition.

items.item: Learnable token embeddings as single matrix multiply on one-hot row; positional embeddings to break attention's permutation-equivariance; relative position embeddings encode offsets, generalize to longer sequences than seen at training
items.notes: Section 3.1 covers token embeddings, sinusoidal vs learned positional encoding, and Section 3.5.2 covers RoPE/ALiBi for relative positions.

items.item: Three architecture flavors with concise comparison: encoder-only (BERT, representation), decoder-only (GPT, autoregressive), encoder-decoder (T5, cross-attention); next-token vs masked-token classification heads
items.notes: Section 3.5.1 covers all three families.

items.item: BERT pretraining: MLM (replace tokens with [MASK], classifier-head reconstruction) + NSP (predict whether two sentences are related using [CLS] context vector); [CLS] forced to summarize the whole input; joint loss = MLM + NSP
items.notes: Section 1.4 mentions BERT pretraining in passing. The book does not have a focused walkthrough of MLM + NSP with the [CLS] sentence-embedding interpretation. Consider adding to Section 1.4 or a dedicated BERT subsection in Part 2.

items.item: [CLS] context vector used as a sentence embedding for downstream tasks; alternative is mean pooling of all context vectors
items.notes: Book does not explicitly cover [CLS] as a sentence embedding mechanism. This is foundational for understanding fine-tuning of BERT-family classifiers and should be added.

items.item: RoBERTa improvements over BERT: MLM-only (no NSP), BPE tokenizer, trained on both single sentences and sentence pairs
items.notes: Book mentions BERT but not RoBERTa; the slide's concise contrast is useful pedagogy and should be added as a one-paragraph 'BERT variants' note.

items.item: GPT decoder per-token context vector feeds next-token classifier head; dataset preparation as shifted input/target pairs (tokens 1..n -> tokens 2..n+1)
items.notes: Section 3.2 covers the autoregressive forward pass and shifted training pair structure.

items.item: Encoder-decoder use case (French-to-English translation): encoder produces context vectors for source tokens; decoder autoregressively generates targets using cross-attention
items.notes: Section 3.5.1.3 covers the T5 family encoder-decoder usage.

items.item: Encoder-decoder PyTorch reference implementation: Residual class wrapping any sub-layer; DecoderLayer with three residual blocks (self-attn, cross-attn, FFN); two masks (tgt_mask causal, src_mask padding); top-level EncoderDecoderTransformer
items.notes: Section 3.3 builds a decoder-only model from scratch but never assembles the full encoder-decoder reference implementation with separate self/cross/FFN residual blocks and the two-mask pattern. Worth a dedicated subsection or appendix code listing for readers building seq2seq systems.

items.item: Helper functions for causal target mask and source padding mask (two distinct mask types used together in the decoder)
items.notes: Book covers causal masks but does not explicitly contrast 'two simultaneous masks in the same decoder layer' (tgt causal + src padding). Adding a short note avoids a common implementation bug.

items.item: Label smoothing: cross-entropy on one-hot target encourages overconfidence; assigning small probability to other classes acts as regularization
items.notes: Section 3.4 covers training loop but never mentions label smoothing as a regularizer. Worth a one-paragraph callout, especially since it remains standard practice in MT and helps explain calibration issues elsewhere in the book.

items.item: MoE parameter arithmetic: dense FFN 2048*512+512*2048 ~ 2M params; split into 16 experts of hidden 128 each gives 512*128+128*512 ~ 130K per expert (total still 2M but only 1 or few active per token)
items.notes: Section 3.8.3 introduces MoE conceptually but never shows the parameter arithmetic that makes the case concrete. The slide's step-by-step calc (2M dense -> 16x130K experts) is the single best way to internalize why MoE 'multiplies capacity without multiplying compute'. Add as a numeric example.

items.item: Sparse vs dense MoE: sparse selects a single or a few experts; dense selects all with weighting. Switch Transformer = special case of top-1 selection
items.notes: Section 3.8.3 covers the sparse/dense distinction and Switch Transformer top-1 routing.

items.item: Router/gating network architecture: simple linear layer followed by softmax producing routing weights over experts
items.notes: Section 3.8.3 shows the linear + softmax router and the top-k algorithm.

items.item: KeepTopK routing strategy: always route to all of the top-K experts (vs other variants like single-best or load-balanced)
items.notes: Section 3.8 covers top-k routing in code but does not name 'KeepTopK' as a strategy. Minor terminology gap.

items.item: Load balancing techniques as a system: noisy gating (add noise to router logits), load-balancing auxiliary loss penalizing uneven usage, capacity constraints capping tokens-per-expert-per-batch, temperature adjustment
items.notes: Section 3.8 covers the auxiliary loss in detail (Algorithm 3.8.1) and mentions noisy gating/capacity. Already at greater depth than slide.

items.item: DeepSeek-R1 as MoE example: 671B total parameters, 37B active per token
items.notes: Section 3.8.3.2 lists DeepSeek-V3 with the same arithmetic in Table 3.8.1.

items.item: Gibbs sampling / MCMC framework for variational inference: resample one coordinate at a time from its full conditional p(z_i | z_{-i}); applied to latent-variable models like Naive Bayes mixtures and LDiA
items.notes: Section 4.4 covers diffusion LMs but does not connect them to the broader iterative-refinement / MCMC family. A short callout linking discrete-diffusion denoising to Gibbs sampling (each step resamples some tokens conditioned on others) would deepen the conceptual framing. Bigger gap: Gibbs sampling for LDiA inference is nowhere in the book despite being foundational for topic models.

items.item: Beta and Dirichlet as conjugate priors for Bernoulli and multinomial; conjugacy enables closed-form integration and 'add counters' update rule
items.notes: Outside the immediate scope of Ch 4.4 (decoding), but worth flagging for any future topic-models / Bayesian-NLP appendix. The Gibbs deck is essentially LDiA inference, which the book never covers.

items.item: MCMC practical caveats: burn-in (discard first B iterations), lag (take every Lth sample to reduce autocorrelation), multiple chains from different starts
items.notes: Useful context for understanding why diffusion LMs need 20-50 denoising steps (analog of burn-in) and why temperature/parallel chains are used. Add as a 'Note: Connection to MCMC' callout in Section 4.4.

top_5_must_add: Section 1.2: Add a topic-models bridge (BoW -> topic vectors -> LSA via truncated SVD -> LDiA as Bayesian mixture). The single biggest classical-NLP gap in Ch 1; deck 1122 has the full pipeline.
Section 3.8: Add the MoE parameter arithmetic worked example from deck 1308 slides 3-4 (dense 2M -> 16 experts of 130K each). The conceptual gap that makes 'capacity vs compute' click for readers.

Section 3.3 (or appendix): Add the full encoder-decoder reference implementation from deck 1307 (Residual class, DecoderLayer with three residual blocks, dual mask helpers, EncoderDecoderTransformer). Book builds only decoder-only; readers building MT or seq2seq systems need this.
Section 1.4: Add a focused BERT pretraining walkthrough (MLM + NSP + [CLS] as sentence embedding + RoBERTa variant). Currently fragmented across sections; deck 1303 has the clean version.

Section 1.3: Add the 'generalized embeddings' subsection (graph walks, song-recommendation pipeline from deck 1123 slides 18-21). Memorable, non-NLP application that makes the distributional hypothesis click.
